title: Bias Term
body:
need to add a [[Bias]] at every term

---

Evan's line above is the whole rule: **every [[Neuron]] gets its own $b$.** A layer of $n$ units
carries $n$ biases alongside its $n \times m$ [[Weights]] matrix.

$$
y = \sigma(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b)
$$

It is a learned parameter, updated by [[Gradient Descent]] exactly like a weight, and its gradient
is the simplest one in the network: $\partial(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b)/\partial b = 1$, so the
bias just receives whatever error arrives at that unit.

**Why it has to be there.** Without $b$ the boundary $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} = 0$ passes
through the origin, and a unit can only answer "which side of a hyperplane through zero". The bias
translates that hyperplane anywhere. In one dimension it is the $b$ of $y = mx + b$, which is
exactly what it is: the intercept. A unit with weights but no bias cannot even represent "output 1
regardless of input".

The common implementation trick is to fold it in: append a constant $1$ to the input vector and
treat $b$ as one more weight on it. Then the formula is a pure [[Dot Product]] and the code has one
case instead of two. Worth recognising when reading someone else's [[NumPy]].

Biases can be initialised to zero, unlike weights, because the random weights have already broken
the symmetry between units. See [[Weights]].

## Related

- [[Forward Pass]]: where the biases show up as a vector added after the matrix product
